blocks.text: The **menisci** are two C-shaped pads of fibrocartilage (medial and lateral) between the thigh bone and the shin bone. They share load, add stability and help nourish the joint. A **meniscal tear** can happen in two main settings [Ref - to verify]:

rows: Younger, active; twisting or pivoting injury, often with ACL or MCL injury; the tear may be repairable if it is near the blood supply at the edge of the meniscus
Middle-aged or older; gradual or minor-trauma onset, often with early knee osteoarthritis; many tears cause little or no pain

blocks.text: Meniscal tears are common on MRI in people without knee pain, especially with increasing age [Ref - to verify]. A tear on MRI is not by itself proof that it is the cause of the pain.

items: Pain along the inner or outer joint line, often with twisting, deep squatting or kneeling.
Swelling that develops over a day or two (slower than ACL swelling).
Catching, clicking or a feeling that something is stuck.
**Locking:** the knee cannot fully straighten. A true mechanical block suggests a displaced fragment, for example a bucket-handle tear. Do not confuse with stiffness or pain-limited movement.
Giving way from pain or weakness.

rows: How did it start? Twist, pivot, deep squat, or gradual onset?
Where is the pain, inner or outer side?
Does the knee lock or can you not straighten it?
Does the swelling come and go?
Did it give way, and did it swell within hours?
Past knee injury, surgery, or osteoarthritis?
Fever, hot red knee, or sudden severe pain at rest?
What activities do you need to do?

items: Observe swelling, muscle wasting and gait.
Check effusion and range of movement, noting any block to extension.
Palpate the joint lines.
Ligament tests to exclude ACL, MCL and other injuries.
Meniscal tests (Section E).
Functional tests such as squat and step-down.
Hip and lumbar screen.

blocks.text: Honest note: no single clinical test accurately diagnoses a meniscal tear. Joint-line tenderness, history and test clusters work better than any one test [Ref - to verify]. MRI is requested by a doctor when the result will change management.
E1. Joint-line palpation

rows: Supine with the knee bent to about 90 degrees and the foot supported
Find the joint line with the thumb, just above the tibial plateau, and press along the medial and lateral sides
Localised tenderness that reproduces the familiar pain
A positive result is one of the more useful findings for a meniscal source
Also tender in osteoarthritis, MCL sprain and other conditions

blocks.text: E2. McMurray test

rows: Reproduce pain or a click as a torn meniscus is loaded by rotation
Supine, hip and knee fully flexed

Hold the heel and palpate the joint line. Rotate the shin outward and apply a varus stress to test the medial side; then rotate the shin inward and apply a valgus stress to test the lateral side. Extend the knee slowly while keeping the rotation
Pain and a palpable click or clunk at the joint line
Meniscal tear, particularly in the posterior part, when painful
Moderate sensitivity, higher specificity in some reports; pain alone is less useful than a click with pain [Ref - to verify]
Moving too fast; not holding the rotation; counting general pain as positive

blocks.text: E3. Thessaly test

rows: Reproduce symptoms with a weight-bearing rotational load
Standing on the affected leg, holding the therapist's hands for balance; knee bent to about 20 degrees
The patient twists the body and knee inward and outward three times
Pain or a sense of catching or locking at the joint line
Meniscal tear when combined with joint-line tenderness
Reported accuracy varies between studies [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: E4. Extension block check

Compare passive knee extension on both sides. A springy block with a firm sensation on attempted extension suggests a mechanical block, while a pain or swelling limit has a soft sensation. Document and refer if there is a true block.
E5. Combining

Findings that together raise the likelihood of a meniscal tear include a twisting history, joint-line tenderness, a positive McMurray or Thessaly test, and a true locking history. Findings that favour OA include older age and gradual onset. MRI is considered by a doctor.

rows: Pop, rapid swelling, giving way, positive Lachman

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Locked knee: true block to full extension
Displaced tear fragment blocking joint movement
**Urgent to semi-urgent** (early surgical opinion; the sooner the better)
Do not force the knee; refer to orthopaedics
Hot red swollen knee with fever
Gross instability, severe swelling, history of high-energy injury
Check foot pulses and sensation; emergency services
Inability to bear weight, bony tenderness, deformity

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
True mechanical block (locked knee)? **Yes:** urgent orthopaedic referral.

Twisting injury with joint-line pain and positive tests, no locking? **Yes:** working diagnosis is suspected traumatic meniscal tear. Screen for ACL and other injuries and discuss imaging with a doctor.
Older patient with gradual joint-line pain and osteoarthritis features? **Yes:** working diagnosis is degenerative meniscal tear in the context of knee OA. Start exercise-based care.
Persisting mechanical symptoms (true catching or locking) despite good rehabilitation? **Yes:** orthopaedic review.

rows: Stiffness without a true mechanical block
Pain increases or a mechanical block is found

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education and exercise. Manual therapy is a minor adjunct. Do not use manipulation or forced rotation techniques on a suspected meniscal tear. Do not claim that manual therapy can reposition a torn meniscus.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** for degenerative tears and many stable traumatic tears, exercise therapy is a first-line treatment [Ref - to verify]. Trials have shown that, for many people with a degenerative tear, exercise therapy gives results similar to arthroscopic partial meniscectomy and that surgery is not better for most [Ref - to verify]. Follow surgeon instructions after surgery.

rows: Heel slides and gentle range work
Slide the heel toward the buttock, then straighten
10 reps, a few times a day
Quadriceps sets and straight leg raise
Tighten the thigh and lift the straight leg
Knee bend to about 60 degrees at first
Graded walk-to-run, then change of direction

blocks.text: **Early avoidance:** deep squats, kneeling and twisting on a planted foot until the knee tolerates daily activity without swelling or catching. No fixed date is set for returning to sport; use the criteria: no swelling, full range, good strength and control, and no mechanical symptoms [Ref - to verify].

**After meniscal repair:** protocols restrict weight-bearing, range and deep flexion for a period that depends on the repair type, so follow the surgeon. Return to sport is usually later than after partial meniscectomy [Ref - to verify].
**After partial meniscectomy:** rehabilitation is usually quicker, with progression guided by swelling and function.

rows: Not routinely recommended; surgeon directed after repair

items: **Visit 1:** screen flags and the extension block, check for ACL and MCL injury, explain the condition.
**Early:** control swelling, restore range, activate the quadriceps, walk normally.
**Middle:** progress strength and function with limited deep flexion under load at first.
**Late:** return to sport or work with graded loading and control.
**If no improvement or true mechanical symptoms:** orthopaedic review for imaging and the option of surgery (repair or partial meniscectomy).

blocks.text: Record swelling, range of movement (especially extension), joint-line pain, catching or locking episodes, strength, functional tests, the KOOS and a 0 to 10 pain scale [Ref - to verify].

rows: Pain and swelling decreasing, strength improving
No improvement after about 3 months of good exercise
Review the diagnosis; consider imaging and specialist opinion

blocks.text: **Case:** A 52-year-old woman has 3 weeks of inner knee pain after a deep squat while gardening. It swelled a little the next day. She feels catching when she turns and she can fully straighten the knee. Joint-line tenderness is present on the inner side and McMurray reproduces pain and a click. Lachman is normal. No fever.

**Working diagnosis:** medial meniscal tear, probably degenerative. **Plan:** education, exercise therapy for strength and function, avoid deep squats and twisting at first, reassess in 2 weeks, orthopaedic review if true locking or no improvement.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why is an MRI tear not enough to decide on surgery? Tears are common in people without pain and many degenerative tears improve with exercise, so symptoms and function guide the decision [Ref - to verify].
How do you tell true locking from pain-limited movement? A true block is a mechanical stop with a firm sensation, while pain-limited movement improves with relaxation and is softer.
A 20-year-old has a locked knee after a twist. What next? Urgent orthopaedic referral, because a displaced tear may need early surgery to protect the joint.
Why avoid deep squats initially? They load and compress the menisci and may provoke symptoms in a tear.
Why also test the ACL? ACL injuries often come with meniscal tears and change the treatment plan.
**Initial approach:** screen for a locked knee, then education and exercise therapy.
**Justifying findings:** joint-line tenderness, twisting history, positive tests, no true block.
**Priority:** restore range, strength and function.
**Manual therapy:** minor adjunct.
**Exercise:** range, quadriceps and hip strengthening, graded function.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** many tears improve without surgery, and surgery is reserved for specific situations.
**Avoid:** forced rotation, deep loaded squats early, ignoring a true block.
**Measure:** swelling, range, pain, strength, KOOS.
**If no improvement:** orthopaedic review.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** swelling-free function, return-to-activity criteria met.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** no true locking, no major ligament injury, no infection.

items: **Can be tested:** whether exercise therapy matches surgery for degenerative tears; which traumatic tears benefit from repair.
**Hypotheses:** that meniscal load management protects the joint.
**Future questions:** best rehabilitation after repair; which patients should be offered surgery first.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Explain the difference between traumatic and degenerative tears.
Perform joint-line palpation, McMurray and Thessaly tests and state their limits.
Recognise a locked knee and refer promptly.
Build a starting exercise plan with clear progression rules.
